lines.text: A country named for the line around the middle of the Earth, with snow-capped volcanoes, Amazon forest and islands that changed science. This is Ecuador.
About four million years ago, volcanoes in the Pacific raised the oldest of today's Galapagos Islands from the sea.
On the mainland coast, more than five thousand years ago, the Valdivia people made some of the first pottery of the Americas.
In the late fourteen hundreds the Inca marched north from Cusco and made these highlands part of the greatest empire of the Americas.
Atahualpa won a civil war against his half-brother, only to be captured by Pizarro's small Spanish force, ransomed, and executed in 1533.
Over the Andes rises Cotopaxi, one of the highest active volcanoes on Earth.
On the Pacific, the Spanish founded Guayaquil, which would grow into the country's largest city and main port.
High in the mountains, they rebuilt Quito as their capital, and its old town is still one of the best kept in the Americas.
Around 1800 the German naturalist Alexander von Humboldt explored these lands, climbing volcanoes and seeing nature as one connected web.
Antonio Jose de Sucre, a Venezuelan general and Bolivar's right hand, would one day free Ecuador from Spain.
In 1802 Humboldt climbed high on Chimborazo, whose summit is the farthest point from the centre of the Earth.
In 1835 a young Englishman, Charles Darwin, studied the wildlife of the Galapagos. What he saw helped lead him to evolution.
The fight for freedom began with Quito's revolt in 1809, and ended in 1822, when Sucre won on the slopes of Pichincha.
Ecuador joined Bolivar's great republic, Gran Colombia, but rivalries soon broke it apart.
Ecuador went its own way in 1830, a nation of the Andes, the Amazon and the Galapagos.
Eloy Alfaro, a liberal president, built the railway that at last linked Quito to the coast.
Rafael Correa would lead the country for a decade, from 2007 to 2017.
And Daniel Noboa would become president in 2023, still in his thirties.
In 2008 Ecuador wrote a new constitution, the first in the world to give rights to nature itself.
In 2016 a strong earthquake struck the coast, and some six hundred and seventy people died.
From ancient pottery to the rights of nature, Ecuador's story runs right along the middle of the world.
